book.title: When: The Scientific Secrets of Perfect Timing
book.author: Daniel H. Pink

confidence_note: The old Hemingway routine is not attributable to When and was removed. The tweets study, earnings calls and the analytic/insight split are confirmed through reviews, reader highlights and summaries; no full text was available. Chronotype detail kept general. Twitter study figures follow press reports of Golder and Macy.
facts: Pink opens with a Cornell study of about 500 million tweets from about 2.4 million people in 84 countries over two years.
Positive language rose in the morning, dropped in the afternoon and rose again in the evening, across continents and time zones: peak, trough, rebound.
An analysis of more than 26,000 earnings calls from about 2,100 US companies found afternoon calls 'more negative, irritable, and combative' than morning ones, and the tone moved stock prices.
Analytic tasks go best at the morning peak for most people; insight tasks go better in the late afternoon or early evening, when the mind's guard is lower. Pink calls it the 'inspiration paradox'.
Larks and 'third birds' run peak, trough, rebound through the day; owls run it roughly in reverse.
Pink's explanation for the insight result: when we are a little groggy, our mental guard is down and stray thoughts get in, which helps the sudden connections insight problems need.
The researchers behind the earnings-call study linked the worse afternoon tone to weaker share-price reactions.

In the tweets study, weekend mood followed the same shape but the morning peak came about two hours later, consistent with people sleeping in; the afternoon decline showed up on weekends too, so it was not only about work.
scene_details: earnings calls turning combative after lunch
tension: The same executives, same type of call: the time on the clock changed the tone, and the market reacted.
opening_idea: Open on the earnings calls: a company's quarterly call is scheduled after lunch.

lessons.idea: Match the kind of work to the hour: sharp analysis at your peak, open-ended ideas when you are a little tired.
lessons.anchor: Analytic at peak, insight at the trough/rebound.
lessons.example: A freelance designer checks invoices and contracts in the morning and sketches new concepts in the early evening.

reflect_final: Which task on your list tomorrow needs your sharpest hour, and when in your day does that hour actually come?

use_cases.situation: Scheduling a tough negotiation or review.
use_cases.move: Ask to hold it in the morning; Pink cites earnings calls turning more combative in the afternoon.

use_cases.situation: Planning a brainstorm with a colleague.
use_cases.move: Suggest late afternoon, when insight work tends to go better.
Put the task with numbers first and the open-ended one later, then compare.

pocket_idea: Afternoon earnings calls ran more combative; schedule your hardest analytic work before your trough.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Executives on afternoon earnings calls sounded more irritable than on morning calls, and stock prices noticed.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Pink starts with 500 million tweets: mood peaks in the morning, dips in the afternoon, rebounds at night. Earnings calls after lunch were more combative. So analytic work at the peak, insight work later.
conversation_variants.question_idea: When in the day are you at your sharpest?
